abstract: ABSTRACT Toward the end of 2022, the cessation of China's “dynamic zero‐COVID policy” had led to a notable outbreak of SARS‐CoV‐2 infections and a substantial number of severe cases and deaths were reported, which raised serious concerns. Concurrently, our study identified a significant increase in the incidence of indeterminate results from the Interferon‐γ Release Assay (IGRA) among hospitalized patients during this period. Peripheral T cells from these individuals were unable to produce measurable levels of IFN‐γ upon stimulation with the PHA mitogen. This indeterminate IGRA results emerged as a potential risk factor for increased mortality among severely affected elderly COVID‐19 patients, contributing to an understanding of the observed excess mortality. The deep serum proteomic analysis elucidated a dysfunctional immune response and defect in cardiac function of those patients. A predictive panel including IGRA results significantly enhanced the accuracy of predicting mortality outcomes in COVID‐19 cases (AUC = 0.9762). We also extended the relevance of indeterminate IGRA outcomes as a risk factor for mortality to elderly non‐COVID‐19 respiratory infections, providing valuable prognostic insights into this type of disease and informing targeted and effective therapeutic interventions for similar outbreaks in the future.

Materials and Methods
2.1
Study Population
The participants were recruited from the Peking University Third Hospital. SARS‐CoV‐2 infection was confirmed by positive detection of SARS‐CoV‐2 nucleic acid by reverse transcriptase‐ polymerase chain reaction (RT‐PCR). All clinical characteristics were acquired from Peking University Third Hospital. Blood samples for research purposes were collected in pro‐coagulation vacuum tubes using standard venepuncture protocols. Serum was extracted by centrifugation for 10 min at 3000 rpm and subsequently stored at −80°C before use.
2.2
IGRA
IGRA was performed using the QuantiFERON‐TB Gold Plus (Qiagen) chemiluminescence assay on the DS2 automated platform based on the manufacturer's protocol. The DS2 was used to quantify the concentration of IFN‐γ in each sample tube. A result of positive, negative, or indeterminate was made using an algorithm per the manufacturer's instructions. The positive control tube uses PHA mitogen to induce an IFN‐γ response and demonstrate that the patient's T cells are functional. A low response to PHA mitogen (0.5 IU/mL) is classified as an indeterminate IGRA result.
2.3
Cytokine Measurements by Luminex
The concentrations of plasma MIP‐1beta, IL‐6, IFN‐gamma, IL‐1ra, IL‐5, GM‐CSF, TNF‐α, RANTES, IL‐2, IL‐1‐β, Eotaxin, Basic FGF, VEGF, PDGF‐BB, IP‐10, IL‐13, IL‐4, MCP‐1, IL‐8, MIP‐1α, IL‐10, G‐CSF, IL‐15, IL‐7, IL‐12p70, IL‐17, and IL‐9 were quantified using the Luminex X‐MAP system (Luminex, Austin, TX, USA) in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions (LX‐MultiDTH‐10, LabEx Co., Shanghai, China).
2.4
Depletion of Highly Abundant Proteins From Serum Samples
The high abundance protein‐depleted fraction was prepared following the previous laboratory protocol [
16
,
17
]. Briefly, 20 μL of serum and 60 μL of buffer A were mixed evenly, transferred into a filter 0.22 μm cellulose acetate certified tube (COSTOR), and subsequently centrifuged at 10 000
g
for 1 min. The filtrate was removed into 29 × 5 mm preassembled plastic springs for High‐Select Top14 Abundant Protein Depletion using a liquid chromatography system (Agilent Technologies 1290). The depleted samples were collected and the protein concentration was measured using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Scientific) following the manufacturer's instructions.
2.5
LEV/SEV Enriched Fraction Preparation
The method was adapted from the previous report [
18
]. Briefly, a total of 1 mL cell‐free serum was used. Large debris and platelets were removed by centrifugation at 1000
g
for 10 min followed by 4000
g
for 20 min. The supernatant was further centrifuged at 20 000
g
for 45 min to collect crude large EVs as the pellet. The large EVs were washed with PBS twice by centrifugation at 20 000
g
for 45 min. The previous supernatant was further centrifuged at 100 000
g
for 70 min to collect crude small EVs as the pellet. The small EVs were washed with PBS twice by centrifugation at 100 000
g
for 70 min.
2.6
LC‐MS/MS Analysis for High Abundance Protein‐Depleted Fraction
The nLC‐MS/MS analysis was performed on an EASY‐nLC 1200 HPLC (Thermo Scientific) coupled to a Q Exactive HF‐X (Thermo Scientific) mass spectrometer. All samples were separated within 90 min on a reversed‐phase C18 column (25 cm × 75 μm, 1.7 μm, IonOpticks). The elution gradient of B was linearly increased from 9% to 27% within 70 min, then increased to 45% within 8 min, followed by an increase to 95% within 5 min and continued for another 7 min at a flow rate of 300 nL/min at 50°C (Mobile Phase A: 0.1% formic acid in water; Mobile Phase B: 0.1% formic acid in 80% acetonitrile).
For single‐shot proteomics with DIA, the MS1 scan resolution was set to 60 000. The MS1 scan range was 350–1200 m/z, the AGC target was 3 × 10
6
, and the maximum injection time was 50 ms. Precursors were isolated with a dynamic isolation width covering 350−1200 m/z. Precursors were fragmented by HCD at an NCE of 28. MS2 scans were acquired by Orbitrap at a resolution of 30 000. The maximum injection time was set to auto and AGC target was set to 1 × 10
6
.
2.7
LC‐MS/MS Analysis for EV‐Enriched Fraction
EV samples were separated using a nanoElute UHPLC spectrometer within 120 min on a reversed‐phase C18 column (25 cm × 75 μm, 1.7 μm, IonOpticks) with an integrated Captive Spray Source. The elution gradient of B was linearly increased from 2% to 22% within 90 min, followed by an increase to 37% within 10 min, an increase to 95% within 10 min and keep for another 10 min in 95% B at a flow rate of 300 nL/min at 50°C (mobile phase A: 0.1% formic acid in water; mobile phase B: 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile). For sample analysis, diaPASEF (data‐independent acquisition‐Parallel Accumulation Serial Fragmentation) mode was used. diaPASEF data were acquired at defined 50 × 25 Th isolation windows from m/z 400 to 1200. The collision energy was ramped linearly as a function of the mobility from 59 eV at 1/
K
0 = 1.6 V s/cm
2
to 20 eV at 1/
K
0 = 0.6 V s/cm
2
.
2.8
Ethics Approval and Consent to Participate
The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Peking University Third Hospital (ethical approval no. 2023‐007‐02).
2.9
Statistical Analysis
OmicsBean software was used for data analysis, including data imputation, normalization, and principal component analysis (PCA). Genefilter was used to calculate the fold‐change values of proteins. A fold change of > 2, a fold change of < 0.5, and a
p
value (
t
test) < 0.05 were used to filter differentially expressed proteins. Heatmap and network visualization were performed using the ggplot2 package and Cytoscape v.3.5.129 implemented in the OmicsBean workbench. KEGG pathway database (
https://www.kegg.jp/kegg/pathway.html
) was applied for pathway enrichment analysis. We also used the circlize package (version 0.4.15) to circularly visualize pathways that are associated with different fractions.
Statistical analysis was performed in GraphPad Prism 9.0. Data are presented as the means ± standard error of mean (SEM). Comparison between two groups was performed by two‐tailed Student's
t
‐test.

Introduction
COVID‐19 is characterized by a wide range of pathological features, including pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), and systemic inflammation. The virus primarily targets respiratory epithelial cells, leading to alveolar damage and cytokine storm, which can result in severe complications and multiorgan failure [
1
,
2
]. In December 2022, the China's end of “dynamic zero‐COVID policy” led to an outbreak of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection and related hospital admissions. More than 60% of local infections were reported, predominantly involving the Omicron variants BA.5.2 and BF.7 [
3
]. The Omicron variant of SARS‐CoV‐2 was reported to have increased transmissibility and reduced pathogenicity [
4
]. In consistency, the majority of these cases in this wave of infection were classified as mild or moderate. However, a substantial number of severe cases and deaths were reported, which raised serious concerns [
5
]. Official reports indicated approximately 60 000 COVID‐19‐related deaths in medical facilities from early December 2022 to January 12, 2023 [
6
]. Among those deaths in Beijing, 80% were in individuals of 85 years and older. This significant increase of death in elderly people compared to pre‐pandemic levels and the first 3 years of the pandemic [
6
] suggested that excess deaths predominantly occurred among older individuals. ARDS, multiple organ failure, and cytokine storm are the leading causes of death of COVID‐19 [
7
]. Risk analyses also showed that patients with certain medical conditions, for example, diabetes, chronic respiratory, liver or kidney diseases, heart diseases, and cancer could be more likely to have severe illnesses [
8
,
9
]. Frequency of underlying medical conditions increased with age; thus, patients older than 60 were considered in a high‐risk category for serious illness from the COVID‐19 [
10
]. Apart from these, the impact of SARS‐CoV‐2 on the rising mortality rate in elderly patients remains an area requiring further exploration, which is vital for the development of precision interventions aimed at reducing mortality of elder patients, particularly in the post “zero COVID policy” era.
Interferon‐γ release assays (IGRAs) are widely used in public health practice to diagnose latent tuberculosis. In IGRA, a positive control using phytohemagglutinin (PHA) mitogen to induce an IFN‐γ response quantitated by ELISA is available to ensure the functionality of the patient's T cells. A lack of response to the mitogen (< 0.5 IU/mL), which indicates defect of patient's T cell function, was classified as indeterminate IGRA, while acceptable response to mitogen (> 0.5 IU/mL) was classified as determinate IGRA. Multiple studies have shown an increase in the number of indeterminate IGRA patients hospitalized for SARS‐CoV‐2 [
11
,
12
] and a slight increase of mortality rate in this group of patients [
13
,
14
]. The indeterminate IGRA was correlated to reduced number of lymphocytes or impaired peripheral T‐cell status characterized by cell counts or cytokine secretion [
12
,
13
,
14
,
15
]. However, no detailed analysis or mechanisms on molecular level was known.
In the present study, we found that the frequency of indeterminate IGRA increased during the outbreak of COVID‐19 early December 2022 to January 12, 2023. We investigated the implications of T cell dysfunction, as evidenced by indeterminate IGRAs, on the mortality risk associated with COVID‐19 among elderly Chinese population. We incorporated clinical indices and deep serum proteomic analysis and elucidated a dysfunctional immune response, especially the compromised Type 1 helper T (Th1) immune response in those patients. Additionally, there was an indication of potential cardiac dysfunction. We developed a predictive panel, utilizing IGRA result, to enhance the accuracy of prognostications regarding mortality outcomes in COVID‐19 cases. Furthermore, our epidemiological findings suggested that the risk factor of indeterminate IGRA, with respect to mortality, extended beyond COVID‐19 to encompass elderly respiratory infection patients. Our study underscored the critical role of T cell functionality assessment, through IGRA, in the clinical management and outcome prediction of COVID‐19 and potentially non‐COVID‐19 respiratory infection in elderly patients.

3
Results
3.1
Indeterminate IGRA Increased in COVID‐19 Patients and Acted as a Risk Factor of Mortality Among Elderly Patients
Our retrospective analysis of 24 378 patients undertaken IGRA from January 2021 to October 2023 revealed a significant increase in indeterminate IGRA from December 2022 to January 2023, rising from baseline of 6.9% to 18.2% (Figure
1a
) (Supplementary Information S3: 1). The baseline observed in our study is consistent with 8% of indeterminate IGRA patients from a retrospective study of 3002 individuals [
19
]. Meanwhile, we observed a correlation between the surge in indeterminate IGRA and the increase in SARS‐CoV‐2 infections (Figure
1a
). It is worth noting that the baseline of indeterminate IGRA diagnosed as respiratory infection is higher than that of indeterminate IGRA diagnosed as non‐respiratory infection, indicating that infection is more likely triggering reduction in interferon‐γ secretion from T cells to some extent (Figure
1b
). However, we still observed a significant increase in the percentage of indeterminate IGRA during December 2022 and January 2023 (Figure
1b
), indicating a specific impact of SARS‐CoV‐2 infection on peripheral T cell counts or their functionality to generate IFN‐γ. Incidence of indeterminate IGRA escalated with age, especially notable in patients over 80 (Figure
1c
). The follow‐up study indicated that COVID‐19 patients with indeterminate IGRA over 80 faced a significantly higher risk of mortality, underscoring that a specific increase in indeterminate IGRA particularly among the elderly is a risk factor for mortality (Figure
1d
). Thus, SARS‐CoV‐2 infection increased the number of indeterminate IGRA patients, which contributed to the excess death of these population.

(a) Ratio of indeterminate Interferon‐γ Release Assay (IGRA) population (orange line) to total patients tested for IGRA from Jan. 2020 to Oct. 2023. Prevailing SARS‐CoV‐2 infection in Dec. 2022 and Jan. 2023 were marked with red arrows. (b) Ratio of indeterminate IGRA population with infectious disease to total IGRA tested patients with infectious disease (green line) and percentage of indeterminate IGRA population diagnosed with other diseases (blue line) to total IGRA tested patients diagnosed with other diseases from Jan. 2020 to Oct. 2023. Prevailing SARS‐CoV‐2 infection in Dec. 2022 and Jan. 2023 were marked with red arrows. (d) Kaplan‐Meier survival curves for COVID‐19 patients over 80 years old with indeterminate IGRA (IGRA ×) or determinate IGRA (IGRA ✓). *

< 0.05.
3.2
Clinical Characterization of COVID‐19 Patients With Indeterminate IGRA
To further explore the features of COVID‐19 patients with indeterminate IGRA, we recruited a subset of hospitalized SARS‐CoV‐2‐positive patients from December 2022 to January 2023 (Supporting Information S2: Table
S1
). Patients treated with immunosuppressive medications or had pre‐existing immunosuppressive comorbidities were excluded. IGRA results were obtained upon admission. A significant proportion of these patients (28 out of 52 patients) could not generate acceptable IFN‐γ response to PHA stimulation (Figure
2a
), causing IGRA indeterminate results. This subgroup of patients showed a higher mortality risk compared to those with determinate IGRA results (Figure
2c
), consistent with the above findings. It is worth noting that all non‐survivors were in the IGRA indeterminate group. The patients displayed a variety of clinical phenotypes, many of which showed statistically significant correlations with IGRA results, particularly in terms of leukocyte profiling, cytokine profiling as well as heart, kidney, and liver function indicators (Figure
2d
and Supporting Information S1: Figure
S1a
). Notably, a significant increase in neutrophil counts, neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio, IL‐6 level and reduced number of lymphocytes, monocytes and eosinophils were observed in indeterminate IGRA patients (Figure
2d,e
). Among the indeterminate IGRA patients, three were diagnosed as lymphopenia. Intriguingly, the percentage of indeterminate IGRA (18.2%) in December 2022 to January 2023 is much higher than 9.5% from HIV‐infected patients with CD4
+
cells less than 100 cells/µL [
20
] (Figure
1b
), suggesting lymphopenia could not fully account for the indeterminate IGRA in COVID‐19 patients. It could be possible that impaired peripheral T‐cell function contributed to indeterminate IGRA in COVID‐19 patients [
21
]. Differences in lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), urea, cholinesterase (ChE), and N‐terminal pro‐brain natriuretic peptide (NT‐proBNP) were also observed, suggesting potential multiorgan involvement (Figure
2e
).

(b) Clinical tests of APACH II scores of indicated groups. (c) Kaplan‐Meier survival curves for recruited patients with indeterminate IGRA or determinate IGRA. (d) Pearson correlations between indicated clinical tests and IFN‐γ level responses to PHA stimulation. (e) The levels of indicated clinical tests in indeterminate IGRA and determinate IGRA groups. (f) The levels of indicated clinical tests in determinate IGRA groups, survivors and non‐survivors of indeterminate IGRA groups. (g) The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve for indicated tests. **

< 0.01.
The Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II (APACHE II), which was used as a disease severity indicator, did not correlate with IGRA results and was not distinguishable among indeterminate or determinate groups (Figure
2b
and Supporting Information S1: Figure
S1a
). Thus, IGRA might serve as a sensitive predictor of patient's outcome. It is worth noting that although IL‐6 levels slightly increased in the indeterminate IGRA group, other cytokines did not show significant alterations, indicating a loose association between IGRA results and serum cytokine levels (Supporting Information S1: Figure
S1b
). However, a remarkable increase in IL‐6, IL‐8, IL‐10 and alteration of ferritin, LDH, lymphocyte counts and neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio were noted in non‐survivors among indeterminate IGRA patients, suggesting that defects in T cell response and uncontrolled cytokine release should be considered together when determining COVID‐19 outcomes. Furthermore, a biomarker combination including IL‐6, IL‐8, and IGRA results showed high predictive accuracy for mortality with an AUC value of 0.9762 (95% CI: 0.9211–1) (Figure
2g
). We controlled for potential confounding factors such as chronic diseases in our analysis to ensure minimum effects of these chronic diseases to the result (Supporting Information S2: Table
S1
).
3.3
Serum Deep Proteomics to Characterize the Molecular Features of Patients With Indeterminate IGRA
Mass spectrometry (MS)‐based proteomics enables the systematic investigation of circulating proteins which sheds light on host responses to SARS‐COV‐2 infection [
17
,
22
,
23
,
24
,
25
]. We collected serum samples from the above 28 patients of determinate IGRA and 24 patients of indeterminate IGRA, along with 27 healthy controls matched for age and gender (Supporting Information S3:
2
). We carried out DIA mass spectrometry to quantify serum with high abundance protein immuno‐depleted (immunodepleted), serum large extracellular vesicle (LEV)‐enriched fraction and small extracellular vesicle (SEV)‐enriched fraction, all from the same batch of samples, aiming to reach in‐depth characterization of molecular features of indeterminate IGRA patients. In total, 237 samples were analyzed and a total of 6610 proteins were quantified among the three fractions (Figure
3b
) (Supporting Information S3:
3
), consistent with proteome size of circulation extracellular vesicles (EVs) [
18
]. The proteomes from healthy controls, indeterminate IGRA, and determinate IGRA were largely different (Figure
3a
). Proteins altered significantly comparing indeterminate IGRA and determinate IGRA were enriched in pathways including complement and coagulation, platelet activation, cytokine–cytokine interactions, and immune responses (Figure
3c
). Notably, Th1/2 and Th17 cell differentiation pathways were significantly enriched in the LEV fractions, consistent with discoveries from clinical indices. It is worth noting that there is only slight difference of IL‐6 but no other cytokines indicating Th cell status were observed in the indeterminate group compared to determinate IGRA group, suggesting that proteomic analysis is more sensitive than cytokine arrays. Intriguingly, the proteomic analysis revealed hints of cardiopathy from both LEV and SEV analysis (Figure
3d,e
), complementing the alteration of LDH and NT‐proBNP levels on a molecular level. Furthermore, proteomic analyses between non‐survivors and survivors highlighted the significance of coagulation, infection, immune response, apoptosis, ECM–receptor interactions, cell signaling pathway, T cell function and cardiac functions as critical factors in the outcomes of indeterminate IGRA patients (Figure
3f
). COVID‐19‐associated cardiopathy was widely reported by other studies [
26
,
27
,
28
]. It is possible that cardiac function is more likely to be affected in indeterminate IGRA patients, especially for those non‐survivors, based on proteomic analysis. Interleukin‐1 receptor type 2 (IL1R2), intercellular cell adhesion molecule‐1 (ICAM‐1), V‐set and immunoglobulin domain‐containing protein 4 (VSIG4), low‐affinity immunoglobulin gamma Fc region receptor II‐a (FCGR2A), and Calreticulin were significantly increased step wisely in healthy controls, determinate IGRA patients, survivors of indeterminate IGRA, and non‐survivors (Figure
3g
).

3.4
IGRA Result as a Risk Factor for Mortality Could Be Extended to Non‐COVID‐19 Elderly Respiratory Infection Patients
The emergence of the COVID‐19 pandemic has offered an unparalleled opportunity for in‐depth analysis of respiratory infection among elderly populations. Our current investigation identified indeterminate IGRA as a significant mortality risk factor among elderly COVID‐19 patients. This finding prompted further examination into whether such a risk factor might extend to non‐COVID‐19 respiratory infection of the population. Subsequent analysis on epidemiological data collected over the period 2020–2022 has revealed that elderly patients over 80 with indeterminate IGRA results exhibit a markedly increased mortality risk when suffering from non‐COVID‐19 respiratory infection, as compared to those with COVID‐19 (Figure
4a
). Additionally, an elevated mortality rate associated with indeterminate IGRA results was observed in both patients with COVID‐19 and those with non‐COVID‐19 respiratory infection (Figure
4b
). IGRA result showed high predictive accuracy for mortality in non‐COVID‐19 respiratory infection with an AUC value 0.9094 (95% CI: 0.8761–0.9427) (Figure
4c
). Thus, indeterminate IGRA result constituted a general risk factor for respiratory infection‐related mortality among the elderly. This underscores the importance of IGRA assessments in the prognostic evaluation of respiratory infection among elderly populations. To further investigate T cell function in patients with indeterminate IGRA results, we used PHA to stimulate whole blood cells from patients in vitro, measured baseline and stimulated cytokine concentrations and calculated the stimulated cytokine levels subtracted by baseline. We collected samples from patients with both determinate and indeterminate IGRA results. Cytokines IFN‐γ, IL‐2 produced by Th1 cells and IL‐13, IL‐10 produced by Th2 cells were significantly induced and higher in samples from patients with determinate IGRA results compared to those with indeterminate results (Figure
4d
) (Supporting Information S3:
4
). This indicated a compromised Type 1 helper T (Th1) cells and a partial defect in Type 2 helper T (Th2) cells in patients with indeterminate IGRA. We also observed a significant decrease of IP‐10, IL‐7, IL‐17, and IL‐9 in samples from patients with indeterminate IGRA.
Figure 4

Discussion and Conclusion
This study highlights the significant prevalence of indeterminate IGRA correlating with the massive SARS‐COV‐2 infection following China's cessation of the “zero COVID policy.” This phenomenon was particularly notable in elderly patients above 80 years, a vulnerable population that requires much closer attention. Additionally, we discovered a strong association between indeterminate IGRA results and increased mortality in these elderly patients and built a biomarker panel including IL‐6, IL‐8, and IGRA results which achieved high predictive accuracy for mortality among elderly patients. This research is pioneering in exploration of the relationship between IGRA results, COVID‐19, and mortality in the Chinese population.
SARS‐CoV‐2 has evolved several mechanisms to impair host immune response, including the inhibition of IFN induction and signaling. Impaired IFN signatures have been linked to a persistent blood viral load and an inflammatory disturbance that contribute to a worse prognosis in severe COVID‐19 patients [
29
,
30
]. By IGRA, we determined that SARS‐CoV‐2 infection reduced the number of peripheral T cells and subverts the ability of peripheral T cells to generate IFN‐γ. IFN‐γ is well characterized to induce undifferentiated CD4‐positive T helper cells (Th0 cells) into differentiated Th1 cells while inhibiting Th2 cell differentiation [
31
,
32
,
33
,
34
]. Decreased production or the inability to produce IFN‐γ may signal a defect of Th1 immune response. In consistency, we found that Th1 cytokines, IFN‐γ, IL‐2 showed a trend of slight decrease in indeterminate IGRA groups (Supporting Information S1: Figure
S1b
). Moreover, there is a slight trend of shift toward the Th2‐based response, with most indeterminate IGRA patients exhibiting significant increase in the Th2 cytokine IL‐6 levels and slightly increase of other Th2 cytokines, for example, IL‐10, IL‐4, and IL‐5 (Figure
S1b
). However, it must be noted that this was not a robust Th2 response. Th1 and Th2 cytokines including IL‐13, IL‐10, IL5, IL‐4 did not significantly increase when whole blood cells were stimulated with PHA in vitro.
A longitudinal evaluation of IGRA in COVID‐19 patients of age 50–63 with an initial indeterminate result revealed that IGRA becomes determinated in the follow‐up visit [
35
]. This suggests that defects in T cell function measured by IGRA might be a detrimental trigger in the acute phase of the disease but tend to recover among younger survivors. However, for elderly patients, especially patients of age 61–96 with average age 79 in this study, follow‐up IGRA tests are crucial to monitor T cell function in the post‐acute phase. Moreover, complications arising from defects in T cell function post‐SARS‐CoV‐2 infection warrant additional attention.
Our study is pioneering to provide deep proteomic analysis of indeterminate IGRA to reach a depth of 6610 quantified proteins. Circulating EVs including LEVs and SEVs are recognized as key players in long‐range intercellular communication, encapsulating a diverse array of intracellular components and exerting significant functions [
36
,
37
,
38
]. The proteomic analysis of LEV and SEV fractions provided valuable data resource for further exploration of these populations. Serum proteomics analysis further showed an enrichment of Th1/2 differentiated pathways with differentially expressed proteins like CD3E, LAT, PLCG1, and HLA‐DRB4. Moreover, proteomics analysis identified several proteins which increased step wisely in healthy controls, determinate IGRA patients, survivors of indeterminate IGRA, and non‐survivors. IL1R2 is a decoy receptor for the inflammatory cytokine IL‐1β [
39
]. It neutralized the pro‐inflammatory function of IL‐1, exerting anti‐inflammatory immunoregulatory role. In addition, IL1R2 is expressed on Treg and involved in IL‐1β regulated Treg development and Th17 differentiation [
40
,
41
]. Moreover, IL1R2 as a neutrophil signature was reported to significantly alter according to COVID‐19 severity [
42
,
43
]. Thus, a stepwise alteration of IL1R2 might correlate with increased severity and mortality. Calreticulin is reported to relate to cardiac pathologies [
44
]. These candidates are potential hints for further mechanism exploration of indeterminate IGRA and mortality.
Our study presented evidence that the role of IGRA as a mortality risk factor in COVID‐19 can be extended to non‐COVID‐19 respiratory infection in the elderly population. Notably, our finding indicated a pronounced increase in mortality of indeterminate IGRA associated with non‐COVID‐19 respiratory infection, comparing to COVID‐19. Given that the epidemiologic data were collected from 2020 to 2022, it is postulated that the discrepancy in mortality may partially be attributed to the allocation of medical resources, which was influenced by the COVID‐19 prevention and control policies in China. Disease‐specific factors might also make contribution which required further investigations. Our finding suggested that IGRA could play a pivotal role in a broader context, particularly in forecasting the clinical outcomes of infection among the elderly cohort. This potential for wider application underscores the importance of further research to validate the utility of IGRA as a prognostic tool in diverse pneumonic.
Apart from the prognostic value of IGRA, our study also demonstrated some limitations of IGRA applications. IGRA may be limited for the detection of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) in patients with active COVID‐19 or other lung infections since the percentage of indeterminate IGRA of these kinds of diseases increased compared to other diseases. Additionally, other IGRAs, such as T‐spot.TB, might be similarly affected in COVID‐19 patients or other lung infectious diseases. Since IGRAs have become one of the preferred methods for high‐throughput screening of patients for LTBI [
31
,
45
], this should be considered when using IGRAs.
